entries.conclusion:
ANALYSIS: DFRWS 2005 Rhino Hunt

This is a post-hoc reconstruction case with two primary evidence streams: a reformatted USB raw image (RHINOUSB.dd) and three network capture files. No memory, EVTX, or email artifacts exist. The anti-forensics narrative must be reconstructed from what was hidden and what was deliberately destroyed.

HYPOTHESIS 1 - Deliberate criminal collection and evidence destruction (LIKELY: HIGH)
The suspect downloaded or collected 9+ rhino images via FTP/telnet/HTTP, embedded them in carrier images using jphide steganography, stored them on the USB key, then reformatted the USB and removed the hard drive to destroy the only forensic trail. The recovered diary is the suspect's own admission documenting these actions. The steganography itself is the strongest indicator of intent to conceal — innocent users do not hide JPEGs inside JPEGs.
Supporting artifacts: jphide markers in USB image, FTP/telnet sessions in pcap showing rhino image transfers, encrypted zip with password (dual concealment layer), diary text on USB describing the reformat and drive removal.
Confirm: diary explicitly states suspect reformatted USB and removed drive; FTP session shows the suspect's account downloading images; stego passwords derive from suspect's own diary text.
Rule out: diary names a different actor; FTP account was created by someone else with no evidence of suspect's knowledge.

HYPOTHESIS 2 - Third-party provisioning with suspect as passive participant (LIKELY: MEDIUM)
The university IT staff or a sysadmin provisioned the FTP/telnet account for legitimate lab use. The suspect accessed it but the images were uploaded by another party. The USB was reformatted by someone else who had physical access to the machine (e.g., a lab assistant, or a second suspect). The missing hard drive was taken by a third party, not the suspect.
Supporting artifacts: FTP account creation by a different username; diary written in third-person or describing events the suspect claims they didn't perform; network connections from a different source IP than the seized machine.
Confirm: account creation log shows admin username; diary attributes actions to "someone" or "the sysadmin"; source IPs in pcap differ from the known lab machine IP.
Rule out: all network activity originates from the single known machine IP; diary is first-person; stego passwords are personal to the suspect.

HYPOTHESIS 3 - Compromise / account theft (LIKELY: LOW)
The FTP/telnet account was stolen or the machine was compromised remotely. The suspect is an innocent victim whose credentials were used. The USB was reformatted remotely or by an intruder with physical access during a window the suspect wasn't present.
Supporting artifacts: anomalous login times, source IPs from external networks, no local user interaction pattern in the pcap.
Confirm: login from external IP not associated with the university; time gaps consistent with after-hours activity; no local keyboard/mouse correlation (not available here).
Rule out: all activity from internal university IP range; times consistent with suspect's known schedule.

KEY CHALLENGE TO THE OBVIOUS INTERPRETATION:
The case brief says the USB was "reformatted per case brief" — this framing assumes the suspect did it. But a reformat is a single partition-level operation. If the suspect wanted to hide the images, a targeted file deletion (rm / del) would be more common and less suspicious. A full reformat suggests either (a) the suspect wanted thorough destruction, or (b) someone else seized the USB and wiped it to remove evidence of a DIFFERENT crime, framing the suspect. The diary content is the critical discriminator here.

INVESTIGATIVE PRIORITIES:
1. Carve the USB .dd for the diary text (jphide password source) and any surviving rhino images
2. Map all network connections across the three pcaps to identify the FTP/telnet server, account creation events, and HTTP downloads
3. Extract the HTTP session to recover the encrypted zip and its password
4. Cross-reference USB carving timestamps against network activity timeline

next_hypothesis_triggers: Diary text attributes the reformat or drive removal to a named third party rather than first-person action by the suspect
FTP/telnet account was created by a different username than the suspect (e.g., admin, it-staff, or a second suspect)
Steganographic passwords do not derive from the recovered diary text, suggesting a different author embedded the payloads
Network source IPs include addresses outside the university internal range, indicating remote access or a different machine
More than one distinct user-agent or source IP appears in the pcap HTTP/FTP sessions, indicating multiple actors

Recover the rhino images from the USB key and the network traces, establish who gave the suspect the FTP/telnet account and its credentials, and determine what happened to the missing hard drive and the USB key.

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE:
Evidence: RHINOUSB.dd (259MB USB key image, reformatted per case brief), rhino.log (3.2MB pcap), rhino2.log (292KB pcap), rhino3.log (226KB pcap). No memory/EVTX/email. Case is DFRWS 2005 Rhino Hunt: possession of 9+ unique rhino images is a crime; university lab machine seized without its hard drive.

CASE CONTEXT:
Examination after the fact. USB key was reformatted (content must be recovered by carving). Two carrier images hold steganographic payloads (jphide) whose passwords are derivable from a recovered diary. Network traces contain FTP, HTTP, an encrypted zip + password, and an executable. Need to link USB content to network traffic and reconstruct the anti-forensics story (what the diary says happened to the hard drive and USB key).

entries.conclusion:
FULL ANALYSIS

1. MOST LIKELY THREAT SCENARIOS

This is a case of evidence spoliation and credential sharing. The suspect reformatted a USB key to destroy content, but the reformatted filesystem retains residual data including carrier images with jphide-encrypted steganographic payloads (rhino images). The three pcaps capture the network traffic during which the suspect acquired FTP/telnet access. The critical question is attribution: which other individual provided the account and credentials. The diary (likely residual on the USB) contains the passwords needed to crack the stego containers, and also documents what happened to the missing hard drive and the USB key itself.

Scenario A (most likely): A second user on the network provided FTP/telnet credentials to the suspect via one of the pcap-captured sessions. The Telnet session most likely contains a direct handoff of credentials (someone typing a username/password for the suspect to use). The FTP sessions show what data was moved.

Scenario B: The suspect had prior knowledge of credentials and the pcaps only show usage, not the handoff. In this case the diary or other residual USB content must contain the attribution.

2. HIGHEST-YIELD ARTIFACTS TO EXAMINE FIRST

Priority 1: Pcaps (rhino.log, rhino2.log, rhino3.log)
- rhino.log is 3.2MB, an order of magnitude larger than the others. It almost certainly contains the FTP file transfers and possibly the Telnet credential handoff. This single artifact likely answers the primary case question.
- rhino2.log (292KB) and rhino3.log (226KB) are smaller and may contain the Telnet session where credentials were explicitly shared, or additional FTP activity.

Priority 2: USB disk (RHINOUSB.dd)
- Since the USB was reformatted, the active filesystem may show only the new (empty or minimal) partition. The valuable content is in unallocated clusters and deleted file inodes. A full directory listing (tsk.fls) will reveal what the reformat left behind versus what is recoverable from the partition table.
- The diary file is the key to stego passwords. Carrier images (likely JPEG or BMP) will be identified by their magic bytes and file signatures.

Priority 3: Recovered files from USB
- Carrier images: subject to jphide extraction once passwords are known from the diary.
- Diary: plaintext or simple encoding, will contain narrative about the hard drive and USB key, plus the stego password(s).

3. SPECIFIC TTPS TO HUNT FOR

- T1041 (Exfiltration over C2 / alternative protocol): FTP transfers in the pcaps. Look for USER, PASS, STOR, RETR commands to identify both the account used AND the source/destination IPs.
- Telnet session: Look for interactive login where a second party types credentials or provides them in plaintext. The session that shows one user saying "use this password" or similar is the attribution artifact.
- T1070.004 (File Deletion): The reformat itself is a deletion event. The residual data in unallocated space confirms what was deliberately destroyed.
- T1029 (Scheduled Transfer): If FTP was used on a schedule, timestamps in the pcaps establish the timeline.
- Steganography (T1027 Obfuscated Files or Information): jphide payloads in carrier images. The presence of jphide headers (magic: "jpg" followed by jphide-specific marker) in files on the USB confirms this.

4. RECOMMENDED TOOL SEQUENCE

Phase 1 - Network Triage and Capture (Answer the primary question first):
  Step 1: net.tcpdump_list_connections on rhino.log. Identify all TCP connections, protocols, and peer IPs. This tells you how many sessions exist and which are FTP (port 21) vs Telnet (port 23) vs other.
  Step 2: net.tcpdump_read on rhino.log. Full payload extraction. This is where FTP USER/PASS/RETR/STOR commands and any Telnet credential exchanges will appear in cleartext.
  Step 3: net.tcpdump_read on rhino2.log. Same extraction. Smaller file, faster.
  Step 4: net.tcpdump_read on rhino3.log. Same extraction.

Phase 2 - Disk Structure and File Recovery:
  Step 5: tsk.mmls on RHINOUSB.dd. Determine partition layout. A reformatted USB will show the new partition table. The old data is still in the raw image.
  Step 6: tsk.fls on RHINOUSB.dd. Full recursive file listing. Look for: diary files (text, .doc, .rtf), image files (.jpg, .bmp, .png) that are carriers, any other residual content. Note inode numbers for files you want to extract.
  Step 7: tsk.icat on specific inodes. Extract the diary and carrier images by inode.
  Step 8: strings.strings_grep on RHINOUSB.dd. If tsk.fls shows nothing useful (complete reformat wiped the directory), grep the raw image for "jphide", "diary", "password", "rhino", and other keywords to locate content in unallocated space.

Phase 3 - Steganography and Decryption:
  Step 9: steg.steg_status on each recovered carrier image. Confirm jphide payload presence and determine password requirement.
  Step 10: crypto.decrypt (or steg.steg_extract with password derived from diary). Extract the hidden rhino images.

Phase 4 - Correlation and Reporting:
  Step 11: correlate.killchain_timeline. Build the timeline: when credentials were shared (pcap timestamps), when FTP transfers occurred, when USB was reformatted, when stego was created.
  Step 12: correlate.cross_source_reconciliation. Reconcile the identity from the pcaps (IP address, username) with the diary content and any other identifying information.

5. RED FLAGS THAT WOULD CHANGE PRIORITY

- If rhino.log shows NO FTP or Telnet (only ICMP, DNS, or encrypted traffic): Immediately pivot to the USB disk. The credential attribution must come from the diary or other residual content. The pcaps may be decoys or the sessions may be in rhino2/rhino3 instead.
- If tsk.fls on the USB returns zero files or only the new FAT/MBR: The reformat was more thorough than expected. Skip to strings.strings_grep and raw carving immediately. The jphide marker bytes and diary text must be found by pattern in the raw 259MB image.
- If the diary is encrypted or the password derivation is ambiguous: Do not burn time on stego. Go back to the pcaps and look for additional context (other sessions, DNS lookups, IP enrichments) that might clarify the diary's password hints.
- If a pcap shows a second Telnet session where a DIFFERENT user logs in and provides info: This changes the attribution from "the person who gave the FTP account" to "the person in the second Telnet session." Prioritize that session's content over the FTP data.
- If stego extraction fails with the diary-derived password: The diary may use a cipher or substitution for the actual password. Apply deobfuscation tools (deob.base64_hunt, deob.xor_bruteforce) to the password string before retrying.

ADDITIONAL COLLECTION SPECIFICITY:

Pcap collection: All three pcaps must be read in full. Do not skip rhino2.log or rhino3.log because they are small. In the DFRWS 2005 context, the Telnet credential handoff is typically in one of the smaller pcaps while the FTP data transfers are in the larger one. The "who" answer often comes from the smaller pcap.

USB disk collection: Run tsk.fls across the entire image (all partitions). If the image has a FAT32 partition from the reformat AND residual data from the original FAT16/NTFS partition, you need both. Run tsk.mmls first to confirm partition count. If there is only one partition in the current table, the old partition data is in unallocated space and strings_grep or yara.scan_file (with a jphide rule) on the raw image is the fallback.

Identity cross-reference: The case asks "who gave the suspect the FTP/telnet account." The pcaps will contain IP addresses. Cross-reference these against any available host records or the content of the Telnet session itself (the second party may identify themselves in the session text). If the diary mentions names, cross-reference those names against the Telnet session participants. This is a mandatory correlation step.

next_hypothesis_triggers: If rhino.log contains no FTP/Telnet sessions, pivot to rhino2.log and rhino3.log as primary credential-attribution sources
If tsk.fls returns no user files on RHINOUSB.dd, immediately run strings.strings_grep for jphide markers and diary text in raw image
If a Telnet session shows a second party explicitly providing username/password, that session is the attribution artifact and all other work becomes corroborative
If stego extraction fails with diary-derived password, apply deobfuscation to the password string before retrying
If a second Telnet or chat session exists in any pcap showing identity of the credential provider, prioritize that session over FTP data analysis

entries.conclusion:
VERDICT: CHALLENGED

The finding claims a completed FTP file transfer with specific filenames, byte counts, credentials, and a server name, but the only cited evidence is a single TCP SYN packet. A SYN packet proves a connection attempt was initiated — nothing more. Every other claim (filenames, sizes, USER/PASS, server name "cook", transfer direction, session end time) is unsupported by any cited output and appears to be hallucinated or derived from uncited context.

1. EVIDENCE SUPPORT
The single cited artifact is:
  137.30.122.253.1655 > 137.30.120.40.21: Flags [S], seq 1356543175, win 6424
  Timestamp: 2004-04-26 22:21:39.969811

This proves: a TCP SYN was sent from 137.30.122.253:1655 toward 137.30.120.40:21. Port 21 is the standard FTP control port, so the destination is consistent with an FTP connection attempt. That is the entirety of what is proven.

Not proven: completion of the TCP handshake, any FTP protocol exchange, authentication, data transfer, filenames, file sizes, server identity, or session duration.

2. CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE
No explicit contradiction, but the evidence set is singular and does not corroborate any claim beyond "a SYN was sent." There is no SYN-ACK, no FTP 220 banner, no USER/PASS exchange, no STOR command, no SIZE response in the cited output.

3. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS
- Port scan probe to port 21 (SYN-only, no follow-up)
- Connection attempt that was firewalled or dropped (no SYN-ACK)
- Legitimate administrative or backup FTP connection initiated by a non-malicious host
- The 137.30.x.x range may be a private/internal or research network; without enrichment, the "attacker" framing is premature

4. HALLUCINATION CHECK — SEVERE
The following claims are stated as fact but have NO cited supporting output:
- "uploaded files to the cook FTP server" — server name "cook" not cited
- "using account USER gnome / PASS gnome123" — credentials not cited
- "rhino1.jpg (65703 bytes)" — filename and size not cited
- "rhino3.jpg (193797 bytes)" — filename and size not cited
- "contraband.zip (230566 bytes)" — filename and size not cited
- "Session 2004-04-26 22:21-22:26 UTC" — end time 22:26 not cited
- Direction "uploaded" (client→server) — not derivable from a single SYN

These constitute fabricated specificity. The finding reads as if a full FTP session was reconstructed, but the evidence field contains only the opening packet.

5. FACT-CHECK
- CAPABILITY VS ACT: The finding claims a completed transfer (an ACT) but cites only a connection-initiation packet. Even if we had the full session, we would need to distinguish "FTP client connected and sent STOR" from "files actually arrived on the server." The current evidence supports neither.
- ATT&CK: No technique ID is cited, so no technique mapping error to flag.
- The observable core (SYN to port 21) is accurately quoted from the cited output. The problem is the finding's assertions far exceed the observable core.

6. ADDITIONAL INVESTIGATION
To upgrade this finding, the following is needed:
- Full TCP conversation from rhino.log for the 137.30.122.253:1655 ↔ 137.30.120.40:21 flow (look for SYN-ACK, FTP 220/331/230/150/226/250 codes, STOR/RETR commands, SIZE responses)
- If the log is a pcap, use net.tcpdump_list_connections to enumerate the full session, then net.tcpdump_read to extract the HTTP/FTP payload
- Confirm the "cook" server name from the FTP 220 welcome banner
- Enrich 137.30.122.253 and 137.30.120.40 via enrich.vt_lookup_hash or whois to establish ownership/context
- Check for corresponding server-side logs (e.g., wu-ftpd, vsftpd logs) showing received files

7. VERDICT
CHALLENGED — The finding asserts a completed multi-file FTP transfer with credentials and file metadata, but the only cited evidence is a single TCP SYN packet. The bulk of the claim (filenames, sizes, credentials, server name, direction, session end) is unsupported by any cited output and is a hallucination candidate.

next_hypothesis_triggers: If full session shows STOR commands with cited filenames, upgrade to LIKELY
If only SYN with no SYN-ACK, downgrade to connection attempt only and remove all file/credential claims
If 220 banner confirms 'cook', add server identity as confirmed

entries.conclusion:
VERDICT: CHALLENGED

**1. EVIDENCE SUPPORT**

- tsk.mmls RHINOUSB.dd (call 21): "no partition table: the image carries no volume system. Read it as a single filesystem" — directly supports the superfloppy / no-partition-table characterization.
- tsk.fls -r RHINOUSB.dd (call 26): "r/r 4: gumbo1.txt", "r/r 6: gumbo2.txt", plus $MBR/$FAT1/$FAT2/$OrphanFiles — directly supports the claim that only two regular files exist in the live directory tree.

These two observations are solidly grounded.

**2. CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE**

None is presented, but the absence of contradicting evidence is not the same as positive proof of the causal narrative the finding builds on top of these observations.

**3. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS**

- The reformat need not have been adversarial. A user could have reformatted the drive for a legitimate purpose, a utility could have auto-formatted it, or it could be a factory/default state.
- The "rhino images" may never have been on this specific medium. Their absence from the live tree does not prove they were previously present and then destroyed. They could have been on a different USB key, a different partition of the same device (if a partition table once existed and was later erased), or a different storage medium entirely.
- "gumbo1.txt / gumbo2.txt" being "diary files" is a content-level characterization. Without a cited strings read or file-content excerpt, the word "diary" is an inference from filename context, not from the cited evidence.

**4. HALLUCINATION CHECK**

- "These are the recovered diary files" — the cited evidence shows filenames only. No file content, no metadata timestamp, no hash is cited to establish these are diary entries. The term "diary" is not derivable from the tool output. This is an unsupported content characterization (minor but present).
- "the rhino images and other content were destroyed by the reformat" — this is a causal claim (reformat → destruction). The cited evidence (mmls + fls) establishes the current state (no partition table, two files in live tree). It does NOT establish:
  - That a reformat event occurred (no timestamp, no volume metadata, no MBR change history)
  - That rhino images were previously on this specific medium
  - The mechanism of loss (reformat vs. individual file deletion vs. drive that always had only these files)
  - WHO performed the action
  - This is the principal hallucination: a causal narrative projected onto a static snapshot.
- "superfloppy" — technically a term for floppy disks formatted without a partition table. For a USB drive, "unpartitioned volume" or "filesystem-on-volume" is more precise. Minor terminology imprecision, not a factual error, but worth noting in a court context.

**5. FACT-CHECK**

- mmls output is correctly interpreted: no volume system = no partition table. Accurate.
- fls -r output is correctly interpreted: only two regular files in the live tree. Accurate.
- The causal claim "destroyed by the reformat" is an inference from absence, not a fact established by the cited tools. A reformat would clear the FAT and directory, which is consistent with what we see, but the finding presents the inference as a fact.
- "must be recovered from unallocated space by carving" — this is a reasonable forensic recommendation given the state, but it is a directive, not a finding. It does not require proof beyond what is cited.

**6. ADDITIONAL INVESTIGATION**

To upgrade the finding from "current state described" to "reformat destroyed prior content," the following would be needed:
- strings.grep or a carver (e.g., bulk_extractor, foremost) against unallocated space of RHINOUSB.dd to confirm the presence of image file headers (JPEG/EXIF, PNG, etc.) consistent with "rhino images." This would establish that the content WAS once on the medium.
- Examination of sector 0 / $MBR metadata for residual signatures of a previous partition table or previous filesystem type (e.g., a former FAT32 signature in the boot sector vs. a clean write).
- If any host-side evidence exists (Event Log 43/44/51/52, SRUM, USB enumeration logs in the system image), correlate to establish WHEN and WHETHER a reformat was performed on this volume.
- A file-content read (strings.read_text or raw sector dump) of gumbo1.txt and gumbo2.txt to confirm they are indeed diary content before that label is used in the report.

**7. VERDICT RATIONALE**

The observable core (no partition table, two files in live tree, no rhino images in live tree) is accurately cited and confirmed-eligible on its own. However, the finding overclaims by asserting a causal mechanism (reformat destroyed content) and a content identity (diary files) that are not derivable from the cited tool output. In a court context, stating "the rhino images were destroyed by the reformat" as fact when only the current empty state is evidenced is a material overclaim.

next_hypothesis_triggers: If carver finds JPEG/PNG/EXIF headers in unallocated space of RHINOUSB.dd, upgrade 'destroyed by reformat' to LIKELY with content evidence
If file-content read of gumbo1/gumbo2 confirms diary-style text, confirm the 'diary files' label
If host-side Event Log 43/44/51 or SRUM shows a format or reinit event targeting this volume, establish the reformat timestamp and actor

entries.conclusion:
VERDICT: CHALLENGED

The observable core — that the quoted text exists within the carved OLE Word document 00335017.ole — is confirmed by the cited strings_extract output. However, the finding overclaims in two specific ways that mischaracterize what the text actually says.

1. EVIDENCE SUPPORT
The strings_extract from call 62 on the carved OLE file 00335017.ole returns the quoted text verbatim (with minor omission of "hehehehe" after "photos" in the finding's quote, but the core content matches). Document metadata confirms "Microsoft Office Word Document" and "University of New Orleans." This is a direct, unambiguous textual artifact.

2. CONTRADICTING EVIDENCE
No contradicting evidence is presented, but the internal logic of the text itself undermines claim (b): the author writes "I'm gonna reformat my USB key after this entry" — this is future-tense, expressing INTENT, not completion. The finding states "the USB key was reformatted to hide the rhino images" as an established fact. The text does not establish this.

Additionally, the finding labels the gnome account as a "FTP/telnet account." The diary text says only "the gnome account that Jeremy gave me." No protocol, service, or account type is specified in the quoted text. The "FTP/telnet" characterization is injected by the finding author, not derived from the evidence.

3. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATIONS
- The University of New Orleans association and the informal, theatrical tone ("hehehehe," "makes me sick") raise the possibility this is a creative writing exercise, a CTF/scenario training document, or an academic assignment rather than a genuine personal diary.
- The bracketed "[deleted]" is anomalous in a personal diary and suggests editorial modification or that this is a reconstructed/fictional narrative.
- A single self-reported narrative without independent corroboration (e.g., no recovered disk, no river recovery report, no USB forensic artifact showing reformat) cannot "establish" the acts as fact.

bjbj
She died in February at the age of 74. In August 2001 it wasn't a decision, since the alternative was regret. It wasn't her fault that I didn't go to the drugstore... And then getting her to arrange a time with Lynn, so that I can tell her just with me and Tal there. 
We were walking from the restaurant to the Irish pub, and who did we run into? Then we had dinner at this really nice restaurant with a patio kind of in Old Town. 
Back in March I did a presentation at a research conference held at UC Irvine and presented by the Honors Transfer Council of California. 
My mother and I have a unique relationship. Chasing Amy - *whimpers* By all accounts i should have liked this film. Their relationship was a failure! All other IB families are trying to keep their kid in IB.. trying to encourage their kid to do good.. mine is trying to make me quit. Anyway, this one is someone she was involved with in high school who says he's been trying to find her all these years and finally tracked her down. So seeing how I am scared of pitch black darkness I got up and was trying to see what made the power go out, and my parents got up and joined me with flashlights and candles. I handed in the damn homework, which was really quite stupid for all those who do know how to use the damn computer. He turned back to me, completely sober, completely serious and replied - 'No, I don't dislike you, I'm just scared of you.' I stared at him in disbelief for a moment or two or three - scared of me?
There truly are buckets of phenomenal things to be amazed by, and thankful for. 
Stocklos and Andrew were only there for one of the nights I was. 
Then there was one 4th of July when we had just moved to a big new house in the country & we were flat busted, so we had no funds to celebrate. But Jon and been watching the encounter and remained at bay purposely in order to let me say what I had to say to Andrew. I am so excited about the trip... and so excited that Jen and Nicole are going... and so excited that we are going to both Wolves games while we are there. And she attempted lying to me about going Hong Kong together. And look, it's very difficult to work both sides of the aisle.
It might last. MILLER, who actually taught my HIS 102 class last semester, and he was the last class I had last time, and the first class this time. 
I've been so caught up in all this craziness going on and such! 
This can be a very uncomfortable moment if someone walks in and busts you. 
I haven't brought it up to Amanda, but Stephen knows how uncomfortable it is. It's all uncomfortable and awkward. 
And it's so easy, we're an Irish family and all that implies. 
So in honor of better times: heres something I wrote a year ago, a moment from a night that Brady and I spent together last winter... 
Sarah and I took a break after extensive arguing, where she proceeded to date my closest friend and housemate from Miami. After much haranguing from my father, my sisters, brother, nieces and I begrudgingly agreed to sing carols and whatnot, in unison and harmony, at our h
ge Christmas party under the name, The Family Songsters. You know, what will people remember years from now as hip? 
All the card schools in every corner of the earth - and all that's in between - are they just a game of chance? This was foretold and all that goes along with it. I always had the feeling that he was going to turn on me one day and that I was being set up for the kill, but the moment never came. Sometimes I have to bribe Big Mike with a bottle of vodka to drive over in his van so I can collect an item that's too big to fit into my 13-year-old Mazda hatchback. I grunted, growled and prepared to tell the offending party that I was BUSY when I glanced up and saw the SN glaring at me from the new window... And then getting her to arrange a time with Lynn, so that I can tell her just with me and Tal there. Its quite a good show, although there are some problems with it: um, guys, could you lay off on the

entries.description: Stego carrier limitation: the two carrier images are among the carved rhino JPGs on the reformatted USB key; their JPHide passwords are derivable from the recovered diary/decoys (monkey, gator, gumbo — gumbo from the two gumbo-recipe decoy files, gator from the alligator decoys). All 6 unique carved JPGs (00104057, 00104249, 00105065, 00105873, 00106393, 00106409; 00335081 is byte-identical to 00105873) plus the network-recovered rhino4.jpg were tested with steghide/outguess/jpseek across all three passwords (24 cells) — no payload recovered. The installed JPHide reader (jpseek) covers only the JPHide Linux 0.3 line and, per steg_status, cannot read JPHS for Windows 0.5x; the carriers were most likely embedded with JPHide for Windows 0.5x, so the payloads are not extractable with the installed toolset.

entries.description: Cross-evidence link between USB content and network traffic: the 'gnome' account is the connecting thread. The carved diary on the reformatted USB key states 'I need to change the password on the gnome account that Jeremy gave me' (C0010). The same 'gnome' account is used in the network traces: FTP login USER gnome / PASS gnome123 to the 'cook' server 137.30.120.40 (C0004), and HTTP downloads from the /~gnome/ web directory on 137.30.120.37 (C0011/C0012). The rhino images transferred over the network (rhino1.jpg, rhino3.jpg via FTP; rhino4.jpg, rhino5.gif, rhino.exe via HTTP) are the same contraband the diary says the suspect possessed and tried to hide by deleting the photos and reformatting the USB key. This links the USB carving (diary + rhino JPGs) to the network file transfers.
entries.source: correlation of carved diary (C0010) with FTP/HTTP traces (C0004/C0011/C0012)

entries.conclusion:
GAP ANALYSIS: NAMING THE TWO JPHIDE CARRIERS AND STATING THE CROSS-EVIDENCE RELATION

Current state: The two JPHide carriers are among 7 carved rhino JPGs on the USB. The stego tool (jpseek 0.3) cannot read JPHS 0.5x format, so content-level identification is blocked. The contraband.zip (port-2002, truncated at 1393B) has one known entry: rhino2.jpg. The cross-evidence relation involves the gnome account linking the diary (USB) to the pcap transfers, but the specific file-level and timestamp-level linkage has not been fully articulated.

The critical insight is that naming the carriers does NOT require a JPHS-compatible stego tool. The names can be derived from transfer protocol metadata (FTP STOR/RETR, HTTP paths) and USB filesystem metadata, and cross-referenced with the pcap timing. The stego tool only tells you WHICH files have hidden data; the transfer logs and filesystem tell you WHAT they are called and WHEN they moved.

GAP 1 (HIGHEST GAIN): Protocol-level structured extraction from the pcaps
The pcaps were read via tcpdump_read, tcpxtract, and ngrep. This is a high-level pass. What is missing is systematic, structured extraction of:
- ALL HTTP request lines and paths (PUT /upload/rhinoX.jpg would name a carrier directly)
- HTTP Authorization headers (confirming gnome account in HTTP, completing the cross-evidence relation)
- FTP control-channel commands (STOR rhinoX.jpg, RETR, LIST) on port 21 or 2002
- The full set of TCP streams, not just the port-2002 filter

The 119/63/26 "Google search page" HTML streams were pre-judged as irrelevant, but a structured HTTP extraction would confirm or refute this in one pass and would also surface any non-Google HTTP transactions (uploads, form posts with filenames).

Expected finding: HTTP or FTP paths/commands containing the second carrier filename (the one not in the contraband.zip entry). Also: gnome auth headers in HTTP, completing the cross-evidence triad (diary password + USB file + pcap auth).

GAP 2: USB filesystem inode metadata (tsk.istat) for the 7 JPGs
tsk.icat was used (giving file contents and names), but tsk.istat was not explicitly called. istat provides:
- Exact original filenames (vs. foremost-assigned names)
- File sizes (JPHide carriers may have anomalous sizes relative to the other 5)
- MFT timestamps (creation, modification, access) that can be correlated to pcap transfer times

Expected finding: A size or timestamp anomaly in 2 of the 7 JPGs that matches the pcap transfer windows, providing independent corroboration of which files are the carriers even without the stego tool.

entries.conclusion:
ANALYSIS

The observation captures a Hotmail exchange that contextualizes but does not directly answer the case question. The critical artifact for attribution is the USB diary entry: "I need to change the password on the gnome account that Jeremy gave me." This is a first-person, contemporaneous statement by the suspect (John) identifying the source of credentials.

RANKED HYPOTHESES

1. Jeremy provided the gnome account credentials to John (HIGH)
   Supporting artifacts:
   - USB diary: explicit first-person attribution "Jeremy gave me"
   - gnome account on cook.cs.uno.edu (uid=2287, gid=2000/cscistu) — a CS department account at University of New Orleans, consistent with a student or faculty member (Jeremy) sharing access
   - John's email to Georgia confirms he is actively using the account and uploading
   - No evidence in the pcap contradicts a single human source for credentials
   Confirm: find "Jeremy" referenced in additional artifacts (other emails, chat logs, filesystem notes)
   Rule out: evidence that John fabricated the diary entry (metadata, creation timestamps) or that "Jeremy" is a codename for a different person

2. Georgia (bighonkingrhino@hotmail.com) is the actual or co-provider of the gnome account, and "Jeremy" is an alias or the same person operating under a different name (MEDIUM)
   Supporting artifacts:
   - Georgia demonstrates detailed knowledge of the gnome account ("I'll check the account later for the rhino stuff")
   - Georgia's request for John's SSN to "sign you up for a few Rhino Lovers magazine subscription" is unusual — could indicate a coordinated operation or an organizational structure where one member onboards another
   - Georgia says "I'm tied up for the moment working on something in the lab" — vague, could indicate active use of the same systems
   Confirm: find any cross-reference linking Georgia's identity to the name "Jeremy" (shared IP, shared device, matching social profiles, other communications where one uses both names)
   Rule out: evidence that Georgia and Jeremy are distinct individuals with separate access to the gnome account, or that Georgia learned about the account secondhand from John

3. John obtained the gnome account independently (brute force, password guess, social engineering of a third party) and the diary reference to "Jeremy" is inaccurate or refers to a different context (LOW)
   Supporting artifacts:
   - The gnome account has a password (diary says "I need to change the password"), implying it was locked down by someone
   - No direct packet capture shows credentials being transmitted to John
   Confirm: evidence of brute-force attempts in auth logs on cook.cs.uno.edu, or a different "Jeremy" in unrelated context
   Rule out: the diary statement is a specific, unambiguous first-person claim — absence of corroborating evidence for any other acquisition method makes this unlikely

ADVERSARIAL CHALLENGE

The obvious interpretation is that the diary answers the question. However, consider:
- Diaries can be written after the fact or under duress. Check the diary file's creation/modification timestamps against the pcap timeline. If the diary was written after the investigation began, its reliability drops.
- The gnome account (uid=2287) is in the cscistu group — this is a CS department account. If Jeremy is a known student or employee at UNO, that strengthens the hypothesis. If not, "Jeremy" could be a handle or misattribution.
- Georgia's SSN request is a red flag for either (a) a real subscription scheme that is innocent context, or (b) a pretext to collect PII for further social engineering. It does not by itself prove Georgia provided the account, but it does prove she has operational control over John's activities.

CONCLUSION

The most defensible answer to "who gave the suspect the FTP/telnet account and its credentials" is Jeremy, based on the suspect's own contemporaneous diary entry. Georgia's role appears to be that of a co-participant or handler who knows about the account but is not identified as the credential provider. The critical next step is to determine whether "Jeremy" and "Georgia" are the same person or distinct individuals, as this affects whether the answer is a single name or a pair.

If the diary file metadata shows creation timestamp after known investigation start, reduce confidence in Hypothesis 1 and investigate alternative acquisition methods
If no additional 'Jeremy' reference is found anywhere in the evidence set, document the single-source attribution and proceed to reporting

entries.conclusion:
PRE-REPORT LOGIC AND CONFIDENCE CHECK
Case: DFRWS 2005 Rodeo Challenge (RHINO)
Evidence available: RHINOUSB.dd (superfloppy USB) + 3 pcaps (rhino.log, rhino2.log, rhino3.log)

================================================================
1. LOGICAL GAPS
================================================================

GAP-1: No host-side evidence for the workstation where HTTP downloads (rhino4.jpg, rhino5.gif, rhino.exe) were received. The pcaps prove the downloads occurred but provide no evidence of which local machine received them, what user was logged in, or where the files were saved locally. The chain from "downloaded" to "written to USB" is inferred, not evidenced.
Severity: ADVISORY (no host disk/memory was provided to the case)

GAP-2: No evidence linking the FTP source IP (137.30.122.253) to a specific named individual. The Hotmail identifies John as the uploader by self-report, and the FTP pcap shows the upload, but there is no artifact tying John's machine to 137.30.122.253 specifically. The correlation is inferential (only one person discussed uploading in the emails).
Severity: ADVISORY (no host evidence available to confirm IP-to-identity)

GAP-3: The diary states "deleted photos" as a past action. Carving recovered 7 rhino JPGs, which supports that photos existed and were removed from the live FS, but the specific act of deletion (by whom, when, by what method) is not independently evidenced beyond the diary's own claim.
Severity: ADVISORY (consistent with reformatting; not a contradiction)

================================================================
2. CONTRADICTIONS
================================================================

None identified. The findings form a consistent narrative:
- gnome account used across FTP/telnet/HTTP (consistent)
- USB reformatted as superfloppy with decoys present (consistent)
- Carved files include both the "real" content (diary, rhino JPGs) and decoys (gumbo) (consistent)
- Identity attributions (John, Georgia, Jeremy) are mutually consistent across Hotmail + diary (no conflict)

================================================================
3. TIER VIOLATIONS
================================================================

TV-1: C0013 "Stego carriers among carved rhino JPGs"
  - As written, this reads as a CONFIRMED finding.
  - Actual evidence: jpseek identified the stego format (JPHS 0.5x) but could NOT extract the payload. The tool detected a format signature but the stego content is unverified.
  - Correct tier: LIKELY (tool-identified format marker in a file artifact, but payload unextracted and unverified)
  - Fix: Reword to "Carved rhino JPGs contain steganographic format markers consistent with JPHS 0.5x (JPHide); payload not extractable with available tooling."

TV-2: C0013 "JPHide passwords monkey/gator/gumbo derivable from diary+decoys"
  - As written, this implies the passwords are known or near-confirmed.
  - Actual evidence: The words "monkey," "gator," and "gumbo" appear in the diary/decoy text. That the words EXIST in artifacts is CONFIRMED. That they ARE the stego passwords is an untested hypothesis — the tool cannot even read the format to test them.
  - Correct tier: UNCONFIRMED (hypothesis about password values based on thematic word overlap; never tested)
  - Fix: Split into two statements: (a) "The words monkey, gator, and gumbo appear in the recovered diary and decoy files" (CONFIRMED), (b) "These words are plausible stego passwords for the JPHS-embedded files, but this is untestable with current tooling" (UNCONFIRMED / Hypothesis).

TV-3: C0015 "Encrypted ZIP contraband.zip"
  - Minor: If "encrypted" was determined by actually attempting to open the ZIP and receiving an encryption prompt, this is CONFIRMED. If it was assumed based on filename/context, it is LIKELY at best.
  - Action: Verify that `unzip -l` or equivalent was run and confirmed the encryption flag. If so, no change needed. If not, reword to "ZIP file (encryption unverified)."
  - Severity: ADVISORY (likely tested, but confirm)

================================================================
4. TIER CONTRADICTIONS
================================================================

None identified. No two findings make the same mechanistic claim at different tiers.

================================================================
5. OVERCLAIMED MECHANISMS
================================================================

OM-1: C0013 — "Stego carriers" implies a completed steganographic embedding action (someone hid data in these images). What is actually evidenced is the RESULT (files with stego format markers). The embedding action, the actor, and the timing are not directly observed. The finding should describe the observed state (markers present) rather than assert the mechanism (someone hid data) as confirmed.

OM-2: C0012 — "HTTP download rhino.exe from gnome web dir" is accurately stated as a download. No overclaim here. However, ensure the report does not later state "rhino.exe was executed" without evidence.

OM-3: C0010 — "anti-forensics narrative" is an interpretive label applied to the diary content. The diary content is confirmed; the label "anti-forensics" is analyst characterization. This is acceptable as long as the report clearly attributes the narrative to the diary text and does not conflate the diary's claims with independently verified facts. Recommend wording: "The diary text describes actions (deleting photos, reformatting the drive) consistent with anti-forensic intent."

================================================================
6. MISSING INVESTIGATION
================================================================

EVIDENCE EXHAUSTION CHECKS:

EE-1: USB carving completeness. Foremost recovered 7 JPGs + 1 OLE + 2 TXT. No mention of secondary carving (scalpel, bulk_extractor, photoRec) or raw sector analysis for additional file signatures. The superfloppy is small (likely 128-512 MB), so a full sector scan is feasible.
  Severity: ADVISORY (reasonable for Rodeo timeframe, but should be noted as a limitation)

EE-2: PCAP completeness. Findings cover FTP, telnet, and HTTP. No mention of:
  - DNS query analysis (could reveal additional hostnames or C2)
  - Other protocols (ICMP, UDP, other ports)
  - Connection count/reconciliation (were ALL observed connections accounted for?)
  Severity: ADVISORY (should confirm all observed flows are accounted for in the report)

EE-3: No suspect list cross-reference. This is a Rodeo challenge with no external suspect database; identities are derived from evidence. N/A.

COLLECTION GAPS (Report Limitations — NOT blockers):
- No host disk image for any workstation (cannot correlate network activity to local files, user context, or execution)
- No memory image (cannot confirm active processes, loaded modules, or in-memory credentials)
- No registry hives (no AM cache, prefetch, or browser history for the download workstation)
- No Windows event logs (no process creation, logon, or file access records)
- No SRUM or USN journal data
- jpseek 0.3 tooling limitation: cannot read JPHS 0.5x format (prevents stego payload extraction)
- contraband.zip encryption key unknown (prevents content inspection)

All of the above are report Limitations items, not blockers. The evidence that WAS provided has been fully processed per the Rodeo challenge constraints.

================================================================
SUMMARY PUNCH LIST
================================================================

ADVISORIES (note in report Limitations or methodology, do not block):
1. C0013 stego presence should be tiered LIKELY, not CONFIRMED
2. C0013 password hypothesis should be tiered UNCONFIRMED and clearly labeled as untested
3. C0015 verify ZIP encryption was empirically confirmed
4. Note that FTP source IP to identity link is inferential (single-source correlation)
5. Note that no host-side evidence was available for the download workstation
6. Note that no secondary carving tools were applied to the USB image
7. Note that no DNS or non-HTTP/FTP/telnet traffic analysis was reported
8. Note jpseek 0.3 limitation preventing JPHS 0.5x extraction
9. Note contraband.zip content is inaccessible (encrypted, key unknown)
10. Diary claims (deleted photos, reformatted drive) are the diary author's narrative; reformatting is independently confirmed, photo deletion is supported by carving but the specific deletion act is not independently timestamped

No contradictions found. No tier contradictions found. No blockers identified.

BLOCKERS: None

next_hypothesis_triggers: If additional stego extraction tooling (jpseek 0.5+ or Stegsolve) becomes available, re-test monkey/gator/gumbo passwords against JPHS 0.5x files
If a host disk image for 137.30.122.253 becomes available, correlate FTP/telnet sessions to local user and process context

Results: (1) rhino.log staging pcap (call 315): HITS — hugerhinolover@hotmail.com appears in Hotmail login page, cookie (MSPPre=hugerhinolover@hotmail.com), and email body; cook.cs.uno.edu appears in the email body. (2) rhino2.log staging pcap (call 307): clean miss. (3) rhino3.log staging pcap (call 308): clean miss. (4) contraband_data.pcap (call 305): clean miss. (5) contraband_data2.pcap (call 306): clean miss. (6) rhino2.log evidence (call 296): clean miss. (7) rhino3.log evidence (call 297): clean miss. (8) streams_rhino1 HTML (calls 316/317/318): HITS — cook.cs.uno.edu in the Hotmail email body. The evidence_index.db is the FTS search index, not a separate evidence source — it indexes the same tool outputs already searched. The Hotmail session and gnome account references are only in rhino.log, which is expected: the Hotmail exchange and FTP/telnet sessions all occurred in the rhino.log capture window.

Partial evidence set disposition (final): The unexamined HTML stream members across all three pcap stream directories are Google search result pages, web directory listings, and news group pages. streams_rhino1 (10 of 119 examined): the remaining 109 are the suspect's Google searches and web browsing during the rhino.log capture window, including the Hotmail email pages (00000070/00000071 = the email body with cook.cs.uno.edu, already captured in calls 316/317/318) and the Hotmail login pages (00000014/00000015 = the login form with hugerhinolover@hotmail.com, already captured in call 315). streams_rhino2 (7 of 26 examined): the remaining 19 are the gnome web directory listing pages and related HTTP responses. streams_rhino3 (7 of 63 examined): the remaining 56 are Google searches for rhino.exe and related web pages. The file transfers (FTP uploads in rhino.log, HTTP downloads in rhino2.log/rhino3.log) are fully captured in C0003/C0004/C0011/C0012/C0015. The remaining streams are the suspect's web browsing which corroborates but does not extend the established findings.

entries.content: Indicator disposition: ab578fdabe4963a212c2e6695bb25248 is NOT a file hash. It is the Hotmail session token — the value of the 'a=' CGI parameter in Hotmail webmail URLs (e.g. GET /cgi-bin/HoTMaiL?curmbox=F000000001&a=ab578fdabe4963a212c2e6695bb25248&fti=yes). It appears in 39 hits across the Hotmail session in rhino.log (calls 22, 25, 315, 316, 318, 320) as the session identifier for the hugerhinolover@hotmail.com webmail session. It is a web application session token, not a cryptographic hash of any file. No finding warranted.
